You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the test sets up
  - It builds a HelpFormatter with width 22 and calls printHelp(PrintWriter, 22, className, "Header", options, 0, 5, "Footer"). The single option is -x/--extralongarg (no arg) with the description “This description is Long.” The expected output asserts two things:
    1) Usage wrapping: after “usage:” the very long class name is chunked to fit width 22, with continuation lines indented to the length of “usage: ” (7 spaces).
    2) Option description wrapping: since the option label alone already consumes the line, the description starts on the next line and is wrapped; critically, those description lines start with a single space (i.e., the descPad of 5 is ignored once the description moves to its own line).

- How wrapping is implemented
  - printHelp(PrintWriter,int,String,String,Options,int,int,String) delegates to:
    - printUsage(pw, width, cmdLineSyntax): computes nextLineTabStop as the length of “usage: ” plus the position of the first space in cmdLineSyntax. For a bare class name (no spaces), argPos becomes 0, so nextLineTabStop is 7. It then calls printWrapped(...) so the continuation lines for “usage:” are padded with 7 spaces.
    - printWrapped(pw, width, nextLineTabStop, text): builds the wrapped text via renderWrappedText(...)
    - printOptions(pw, width, options, leftPad, descPad): formats options and their descriptions, internally rendering wrapped text for descriptions using a nextLineTabStop derived from leftPad/descPad and the option column width.

  - renderWrappedText(StringBuffer, int, int, String) does the actual wrapping:
    - It finds a wrap position with findWrapPos(text, width, startPos).
    - For continuation lines, it prefixes the remainder with a padding string of nextLineTabStop spaces, then repeats.
    - Two guards exist to prevent the infinite loop described in the issue:
      - If nextLineTabStop >= width, it clamps nextLineTabStop to width - 1 (so there is at least one column left for content).
      - If the computed wrap position falls exactly at the last space of the padding (pos == nextLineTabStop - 1) and the text is longer than width, it forces pos = width so the loop actually consumes characters from the content instead of wrapping only on padding.

    These guards fix the infinite loop where a long, unbreakable token (no whitespace) and a nonzero indent would otherwise cause findWrapPos to keep returning the padding space, making the loop recreate the same line forever.

- Where the failure comes from
  - The usage block behavior matches the expected output given how printUsage and renderWrappedText work: “usage:” is split before the class name (at the single space), then the very long class name is chunked to 22 columns total with 7 spaces of indentation on continuation lines. That yields lines like “       org.apache.comm”, “       ons.cli.bug.Bug”, etc., exactly as expected.
  - The mismatch happens in the options section. With width 22, the option token “-x,--extralongarg” already consumes nearly the entire line; hence the description must start on a new line. The test expects that, once moved to its own line, the description lines are not indented by descPad (5); they start with a single leading space:
    - Expected: “ This description is”, then “ Long.”
    - Actual (from the current implementation): renderOptions continues to apply the descPad-based indent to the description block even when it starts on a new line, causing those lines to begin with the full descPad spacing (e.g., five spaces). This violates the test’s requirement that the description indent be ignored when the description doesn’t fit on the option line.
  - In short, the code fixes the infinite loop in renderWrappedText but the option rendering logic always honors descPad for wrapped descriptions, leading to extra indentation and the observed assertion failure “Long arguments did not split as expected.”

- Summary of root cause
  - Infinite loop root cause (per issue report): when a long word cannot fit and there is indentation, wrapping could repeatedly select the padding as wrap point; renderWrappedText now includes guards to avoid that by clamping indent and forcing a split at the full width.
  - Test failure root cause: renderOptions applies descPad indentation to the description even when the description starts on a new line due to wrapping. The test expects that indentation to be ignored in this special case (use a single leading space for wrapped description lines), but the current code doesn’t implement that exception, so the output does not match the expected format.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
